subject: Tenant migration: IO throttling mitigation & node/storage handoff
messages:
From: Alex Gardner <alex.gardner@medicore.com>
To: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 01 Dec 2027 09:12:00 -0800
Subject: On-prem migration: storage hot spots and tenant move timeline

Jordan —

Thanks again for the call this morning. Two quick asks from our side as we prep the migration onto our prod floor: 1) we see periodic IO stalls on the database-backed inference pods when tenant X runs long batching windows; need guidance on node sizing/tiering to avoid noisy-neighbor effects, and 2) we need a clear handoff checklist for our infra team so they can provision PVs and nodepools without delay.

I attached a small CSV with sample iostat traces from last week that shows the stalls (medicore-storage-metrics-20271201.csv). Can you or someone from Red­wood sketch a minimal node/storage layout and what IO QoS we should enforce?

Target timeline: freeze on changes 2028-01-15, migration window late Jan.

Appreciate any concrete sizing recs.

—Alex
Senior Ops, Medicore Health

[attachment: medicore-storage-metrics-20271201.csv (text/csv)]

From: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Gardner <alex.gardner@medicore.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 01 Dec 2027 11:04:00 -0800
Subject: Re: On-prem migration: storage hot spots and tenant move timeline

Alex — thanks for the traces, that’s helpful. I took a quick pass and pulled a few notes for the infra team; Kimberly and Marissa I’m looping you in so we can align on constraints and an operational handoff doc. High level observations:

- The iostat shows sustained 200–350ms write latency spikes during peak batching windows; likely the PV class is shared across low-priority tenants.
- Two mitigations: isolate inference PVs onto an NVMe-backed storage class for burst writes + set nodepool affinity for heavy tenants; or keep shared storage but apply kube-level IO throttling and strict burst queues.

Proposed next steps (quick):
1) Redwood to propose a nodepool + PV matrix (min recommended vCPU/GPU, ephemeral vs PVC, expected IOPS) — I can draft this.
2) Medicore to confirm whether they prefer dedicated SSDs per tenant (higher cost) or QoS on shared arrays.
3) Exchange runbook for cutover (preflight checks, snapshot steps, rollback path).

I’ll attach a short recommendation PDF and a starter MA­P (mutual action plan) after we sync. Kimberly — can you confirm recommended PV classes for on-prem environments (Ceph LVM, NFS with QoS proxy, local NVMe) and suggested kube IO cgroup knobs?

Jordan Blake
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

[attachment: redwood-nodepool-recommendation-v1.pdf (application/pdf)]

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.ai>
To: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>, Alex Gardner <alex.gardner@medicore.com>
Date: Thu, 02 Dec 2027 08:22:00 -0800
Subject: Re: On-prem migration: storage hot spots and tenant move timeline

Thanks Jordan. Quick notes from infra POV:

- If Medicore can commit to dedicated NVMe-backed PVCs for the heavy inference pods (Tenant X + Y) we can avoid nearly all noisy-neighbor IO stalls. Recommended baseline per GPU node: 1x2TB NVMe for /var/lib/redwood/cache + 1x1TB NVMe for local ephemeral scratch.
- For shared-array deployments (Ceph/Isilon) we recommend provisioning 10k–15k IOPS LUNs and enforcing throttle via Kubernetes device-plugins + Pod-level io.max (cgroup v2) where supported.
- Node sizing: for mixed GPU workloads we recommend (for 1–2k qps per tenant) 8 vCPU + 64GB RAM + 1xA10G GPU (or equivalent). If Medicore expects large batches (token windows >4k) add 2xNVMe per node for KV cache.

Handoff checklist (starter):
- PV classes defined in cluster (name, reclaimPolicy, provisioner, qos parameters)
- Nodepools: name, labels, taints, min/max counts, GPU type
- Storage access: mount options, FS type, iops/throughput guarantees
- Snapshot schedule and retention policy for fast rollback
- Runbook link + preflight health checks (CPU, mem, disk, network egress)

I’ll upload a short template and a sample kube manifest for io.max annotations.

—Kim
Senior Infrastructure, Redwood Inference

From: Alex Gardner <alex.gardner@medicore.com>

Subject: Re: On-prem migration: storage hot spots and tenant move timeline

Thanks Jordan/Kim, useful recs. Medicore prefers to avoid per-tenant dedicated NVMe if we can; budget constraints push us toward shared arrays with QoS. Attaching a short export of our SAN provisioning matrix and a few perf runs — you'll see we can get consistent 12k IOPS on provisioned LUNs but burst behavior is limited.

Questions before we lock the plan:
- Given our SAN numbers, is io.max cgroup enforcement enough to protect production inference pods from tenant Y’s monthly batch job?
- If we use kube-level throttling, what rollback steps do you recommend if we still see tail latencies during canary?

Attached: medicore-storage-metrics-20271201.csv (original) + san-provisioning-matrix.xlsx

—Alex

From: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Gardner <alex.gardner@medicore.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 09 Dec 2027 16:42:00 -0800
Subject: Re: On-prem migration: storage hot spots and tenant move timeline

Alex — got it, thanks for the SAN matrix. Short answers and an actionable cutover plan below.

Q1: Is io.max enough?
Short: It can protect production pods from typical noisy tenants if the underlying kernel and kube version support cgroup v2 and the storage driver surfaces throttling. However, we still recommend layering two controls:
- Pod-level io.max for steady-state throttling
- Nodepool-level tenant isolation using node selectors + taints so the heaviest tenants never land on the same nodes as prod inference pods during canary.

Q2: Rollback steps if tail latency persists during canary:
- Quick rollback: cordon + drain canary node(s), shift traffic to warm standby nodepool (no PV rebind needed if PVs are pre-provisioned on standby), revert kube io.max to previous values, and roll back to previous model/replica count.
- If PV contention is suspected: snapshot PVCs (if supported), move heavy tenant PVCs to dedicated LUNs, or failover to NVMe-backed standby nodes.

Concrete MAP (mutual action plan) items for this week:
1) Redwood to deliver final nodepool + PV recommendation doc (by 2027-12-13).
2) Medicore to add SAN provisioning matrix to shared Drive and confirm whether snapshotting is available in prod (by 2027-12-15).
3) Run a small canary: 1–2 nodes with production traffic + io.max enforced (window: 2 business days) — success criteria: p50/p95 latency within 10% of baseline and no >300ms tail spikes.

I’ll send the MAP as a short Google Doc and the starter runbook snippets to HS-46782. If that plan looks good, we’ll schedule a 60-minute preflight with your infra team next week.

Jordan Blake
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
